chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhl from Yunus ibn Ya'qub said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the man who prays while wearing the burdulah (a type of cloak), and he said, 'It does not harm him.'
Sa'd from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Mahziyar from Ali ibn Mahziyar said:

I wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him) asking him about praying in qirmiz (crimson/red fabric), and that our companions refrain from praying in it, so he wrote, 'There is no harm with it, absolutely,' and 'All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'

key_terms.الْبُرْطُلَةُ: A type of cloak or outer garment, often associated with specific historical or regional styles.
key_terms.الْقِرْمِزِ: Crimson or red fabric, a specific type of textile mentioned in the context of prayer attire.
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm with it (i.e., it is permissible).
key_terms.لَا يَضُرُّهُ: It does not harm him (i.e., it does not invalidate or detract from the prayer).

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pray while wearing red or crimson clothing (qirmiz) or a burdulah cloak?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the fiqh of prayer garments by affirming that wearing *burdulah* (a type of silk or fine fabric) and *qirmiz* (crimson dye) does not invalidate the prayer, thereby resolving the hesitation among early companions. It highlights the Shia scholarly approach of validating common commercial textiles for worship unless explicitly prohibited, emphasizing ease (*yusr*) in ritual purity and attire.
